mod¶

API Signatures¶

DataFrame::mod(other: const DataFrame&) -> DataFrame

DataFrame::mod(other: double) -> DataFrame

Notes¶

This applies arithmetic across the compatible numeric payloads in the current object.

Inputs¶

other : const DataFrame& Second frame, thread, or scalar operand supplied for binary combination, comparison, alignment, or join-style work.

Output¶

DataFrame Value produced by this call.

Options¶

Option and enum values, when present, are listed with their effects under Inputs.

Examples¶

Example 1. Compute the modulus of each compatible numeric cell against another aligned frame.

auto left = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"id", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({1, 2, 3}))},
    {"sales", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({100.0, 120.0, 90.0}))},
});
auto right = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"id", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({2, 2, 4}))},
    {"sales", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({110.0, 110.0, 100.0}))},
});

auto out = left.mod(right);
Expected output¶
id  sales
1   100.0
0    10.0
3    90.0

Example 2. Compute the modulus of each compatible numeric cell against one broadcast scalar value.

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"id", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({1, 2, 3}))},
    {"sales", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({100.0, 120.0, 90.0}))},
    {"city", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_note({"Accra", "Tema", "Kumasi"}))},
});

auto out = df.mod(10);
Expected output¶
id  sales  city
1   0.0    Accra
2   0.0    Tema
3   0.0    Kumasi

This produces a comparison-style result you can inspect directly or reuse as a mask.

Inputs¶

other : const DataFrame& Second frame, thread, or scalar operand supplied for binary combination, comparison, alignment, or join-style work.

Output¶

DataFrame Value produced by this call.

Options¶

Option and enum values, when present, are listed with their effects under Inputs.

Examples¶

Example 1. Compare each compatible cell for inequality against another aligned frame.

auto left = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"id", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({1, 2, 3}))},
    {"sales", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({100.0, 120.0, 90.0}))},
});
auto right = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"id", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({2, 2, 4}))},
    {"sales", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({110.0, 110.0, 100.0}))},
});

auto out = left.ne(right);
Expected output¶
id  sales
1   true
2   true
3   false

Example 2. Compare each compatible cell for inequality against one broadcast scalar value.

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"id", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({1, 2, 3}))},
    {"sales", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({100.0, 120.0, 90.0}))},
    {"city", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_note({"Accra", "Tema", "Kumasi"}))},
});

auto out = df.ne(10);
Expected output¶
id  sales
1   true
2   true
3   false

notna¶

API Signature¶

DataFrame::notna(features: pluss::RangeView<std::string_view> = {}) -> DataFrame

Notes¶

This is part of the missing-data cleanup path and is usually applied before summaries, grouping, or export.

Inputs¶

features : pluss::RangeView<std::string_view> Feature name(s) that select the target DataFrame columns for the operation.

Output¶

DataFrame Value produced by this call.

Options¶

Option and enum values, when present, are listed with their effects under Inputs.

Examples¶

Example 1. Work with a selected feature subset.

auto sales = pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({100.0, 0.0, 90.0}))
                 .with_validity_mask(pluss::make_series({true, false, true}, pluss::ScalarType::Bool));
auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"sales", sales},
});

auto out = df.notna({"sales"});
Expected output¶
sales
true
false
true

Practical Behavior¶

  • notna(...) returns a boolean-style frame marking which cells are observed rather than missing.

  • Use it to build masks before filter(...), replacement policies, or diagnostic summaries.

  • notna(...) and notnull(...) are equivalent.

O¶

observe¶

API Signatures¶

DataFrame::observe(row: std::int64_t, render: bool = true) -> DataFrameView

DataFrame::observe(start: std::int64_t, stop: std::int64_t, render: bool = true) -> DataFrameView

Notes¶

Returns a DataFrameView over a positional row window so you can preview rows from the middle of a frame without materializing a new working copy.

Inputs¶

row : std::int64_t Zero-based row position to preview as a one-row DataFrameView.

render : bool When true, the preview may auto-render in temporary terminal contexts. Pass false when you want to call .show() yourself.

start : std::int64_t Inclusive zero-based starting row position of the preview window.

stop : std::int64_t Exclusive zero-based ending row position of the preview window.

Output¶

DataFrameView Value produced by this call.

Options¶

Option and enum values, when present, are listed with their effects under Inputs.

Examples¶

Example 1. Preview one row without changing the underlying frame.

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"id", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({1, 2, 3}))},
    {"sales", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({100.0, 120.0, 90.0}))},
    {"city", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_note({"Accra", "Tema", "Kumasi"}))},
});

auto preview = df.observe(1, false);
preview.show();
Expected output¶
id  sales  city
2   120.0  Tema

Example 2. Preview a contiguous row window without changing the underlying frame.

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"id", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({1, 2, 3}))},
    {"sales", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({100.0, 120.0, 90.0}))},
    {"city", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_note({"Accra", "Tema", "Kumasi"}))},
});

auto preview = df.observe(0, 2, false);
preview.show();
Expected output¶
id  sales  city
1   100.0  Accra
2   120.0  Tema

Practical Behavior¶

  • observe(...) returns a DataFrameView, so it is the preview-oriented row window helper alongside head(...) and tail(...).

  • It uses positional row coordinates, not case-label lookup.

  • Use observe(start, stop).show() when you want a middle slice without materializing a bespoke helper or mutating the source frame.

place¶

API Signatures¶

DataFrame::place(name: std::string, feature: const Thread&, anchor_feature: std::string_view, after: bool = false) -> DataFrame

DataFrame::place(name: std::string_view, anchor_feature: std::string_view, after: bool = false) -> DataFrame

Notes¶

Moves one existing feature relative to an anchor feature, or inserts a brand-new feature directly before or after that anchor.

Inputs¶

name : std::string Feature name to insert or move.

feature : const Thread& Full thread payload to insert at the target position. Its length must match the frame case count.

anchor_feature : std::string_view Reference feature used to place a newly inserted or moved feature before or after an existing column.

after : bool When false, placement happens before the anchor. When true, placement happens after the anchor.

Output¶

DataFrame Value produced by this call.

Options¶

Option and enum values, when present, are listed with their effects under Inputs.

Examples¶

Example 1. Insert a new feature relative to an anchor feature without rebuilding the whole schema.

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"id", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({1, 2, 3}))},
    {"sales", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({100.0, 120.0, 90.0}))},
    {"city", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_note({"Accra", "Tema", "Kumasi"}))},
});

auto out = df.place("profit", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({40.0, 35.0, 30.0})), "sales", true);
Expected output¶
id  sales  profit  city
1   100.0  40.0    Accra
2   120.0  35.0    Tema
3    90.0  30.0    Kumasi

Example 2. Move one existing feature relative to an anchor feature.

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"id", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({1, 2, 3}))},
    {"sales", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({100.0, 120.0, 90.0}))},
    {"city", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_note({"Accra", "Tema", "Kumasi"}))},
});

auto out = df.place("city", "id", false);
Expected output¶
city    id  sales
Accra   1   100.0
Tema    2   120.0
Kumasi  3    90.0

Practical Behavior¶

  • place(name, feature, anchor, after) inserts a brand-new feature relative to an existing anchor.

  • place(name, anchor, after) moves an existing feature without forcing you to restate the full feature order.

  • When after=false, placement happens before the anchor. When after=true, placement happens after the anchor.

prod¶

API Signatures¶

DataFrame::prod(axis: int, skipna: bool = true) -> Thread

DataFrame::prod(axis: std::int64_t, skipna: bool = true) -> Thread

DataFrame::prod(render: bool = true) -> DataFrameView

Notes¶

Computes per-feature or per-row products across numeric data.

Inputs¶

axis : int Reduction axis. 0 computes one product per numeric feature, while 1 computes one product per row across numeric features.

skipna : bool When true, missing values are skipped during the reduction. When false, missing state can affect the result.

render : bool When true, the summary view can auto-render in temporary terminal contexts. Pass false when you want the summary object without implicit display.

Output¶

Thread Value produced by this call.

DataFrameView Value produced by this call.

Options¶

Option and enum values, when present, are listed with their effects under Inputs.

Examples¶

Example 1. Compute products across rows instead of returning one product per numeric feature.

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"a", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({1.0, 2.0, 3.0}))},
    {"b", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({2.0, 4.0, 5.0}))},
});

auto out = df.prod(1, true);
Expected output¶
[2.0, 8.0, 15.0]

Example 2. Compute products across rows instead of returning one product per numeric feature.

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"a", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({1.0, 2.0, 3.0}))},
    {"b", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({2.0, 4.0, 5.0}))},
});

auto out = df.prod(1, true);
Expected output¶
[2.0, 8.0, 15.0]

Example 3. Compute one product per numeric feature.

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"a", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({1.0, 2.0, 3.0}))},
    {"b", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({2.0, 4.0, 5.0}))},
});

auto out = df.prod(false);
Expected output¶
feature  value
a        6.0
b        40.0

Axis Rules¶

  • prod(render=false) returns a compact summary view with one product per numeric feature.

  • prod(axis=0) returns a numeric thread with one product per numeric feature.

  • prod(axis=1) returns a numeric thread with one product per row across numeric features.

bool_mask : const pluss::Series& Boolean row mask. true keeps or rewrites the corresponding row, while false leaves it out or leaves the original value unchanged depending on the method.

value : const char* Replacement scalar, string, null, or thread written only where the mask is true.

Output¶

Practical Behavior¶

  • put(feature, mask, value) rewrites only the rows where the mask evaluates true.

  • The mask must match the frame case count.

  • Use put(...) when you want a new frame result, and put_(...) when you want the same rewrite in place.

Q¶

query¶

API Signature¶

DataFrame::query(expression: std::string_view) -> DataFrame

Notes¶

Keeps only the rows that satisfy the supplied filter expression or mask-producing query.

Inputs¶

expression : std::string_view Boolean filter expression written against feature names, such as "sales > 95" or "city == \"Accra\"". Rows where the expression evaluates true are kept.

Output¶

DataFrame Value produced by this call.

Options¶

Option and enum values, when present, are listed with their effects under Inputs.

Examples¶

Example 1. Use this overload when its parameter combination matches the result shape or control level you need.

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"id", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({1, 2, 3}))},
    {"sales", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({100.0, 120.0, 90.0}))},
    {"city", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_note({"Accra", "Tema", "Kumasi"}))},
});

auto out = df.query("sales > 95");
Expected output¶
id  sales  city
1   100.0  Accra
2   120.0  Tema

Practical Behavior¶

  • query(expression) keeps rows where the expression evaluates true.

  • Feature names are referenced directly inside the expression string.

  • String comparisons should use quoted values, especially when feature names contain spaces.

ranks¶

API Signature¶

DataFrame::ranks(ties: RankTieRule = RankTieRule::Average, nulls: RankNullRule = RankNullRule::Keep, ascending: bool = true, percentage: bool = false) -> DataFrame

Notes¶

Assigns numeric ranks while controlling tie, null, direction, and percentage behavior.

Inputs¶

ties : RankTieRule Tie policy for equal values: Average, Lowest, Highest, First, or Dense.

nulls : RankNullRule Null ranking policy: Keep leaves null ranks missing, Top ranks them first, and Bottom ranks them last.

ascending : bool Boolean switch that changes how this overload behaves. Read the method notes and examples to see the effect of true versus false.

percentage : bool When true, divide each rank by the number of ranked observations.

    {"city", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_note({"Accra", "Tema", "Kumasi"}))},
});

reindex_cases¶

API Signature¶

DataFrame::reindex_cases(new_cases: const Thread&) -> DataFrame

Notes¶

Builds a new case axis from the supplied labels and aligns rows onto that case order.

Inputs¶

new_cases : const Thread& Replacement case labels in the exact order you want the rows to follow.

Output¶

DataFrame Value produced by this call.

Options¶

Option and enum values, when present, are listed with their effects under Inputs.

Examples¶

Example 1. Use this overload when its parameter combination matches the result shape or control level you need.

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"id", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({1, 2, 3}))},
    {"sales", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({100.0, 120.0, 90.0}))},
    {"city", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_note({"Accra", "Tema", "Kumasi"}))},
});

df = df.with_cases(pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_note({"cs0", "cs1", "cs2"})));
auto cases = pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_note({"cs1", "cs0", "cs2"}));
auto out = df.reindex_cases(cases);
Expected output¶
df.cases():
["cs0", "cs1", "cs2"]

out.cases():
["cs1", "cs0", "cs2"]

out.head():
id  sales  city
2   120.0  Tema
1   100.0  Accra
3    90.0  Kumasi

Inputs¶

new_name : std::string Replacement feature name.

Output¶

DataFrame Value produced by this call.

Options¶

Option and enum values, when present, are listed with their effects under Inputs.

Examples¶

Example 1. Use this overload when its parameter combination matches the result shape or control level you need.

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"id", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({1, 2, 3}))},
    {"sales", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({100.0, 120.0, 90.0}))},
    {"city", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_note({"Accra", "Tema", "Kumasi"}))},
});

auto out = df.rename("sales", "revenue");
Expected output¶
id  revenue  city
1   100.0    Accra
2   120.0    Tema
3    90.0    Kumasi

reorder¶

API Signatures¶

DataFrame::reorder(names: pluss::RangeView<std::string_view>) -> DataFrame

DataFrame::reorder(spec: const ReorderSpec&) -> DataFrame

DataFrame::reorder(specs: pluss::RangeView<ReorderSpec>) -> DataFrame

DataFrame::reorder(specs: std::initializer_list<ReorderSpec>) -> DataFrame

Notes¶

Moves selected features into a new relative position while preserving row data and the untouched feature order.

Inputs¶

names : pluss::RangeView<std::string_view> Column names to move together to the front while preserving the relative order of every column not listed here.

spec : const ReorderSpec& One partial-order move. Use this when one move instruction is enough.

specs : pluss::RangeView<ReorderSpec> Several partial-order moves applied in the exact order you pass them. Each move sees the column order produced by the previous move.

Output¶

DataFrame Value produced by this call.

Options¶

Option and enum values, when present, are listed with their effects under Inputs.

Examples¶

Example 1. Move the named columns to the front while preserving the relative order of every untouched column.

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"id", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({1, 2, 3}))},
    {"sales", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({100.0, 120.0, 90.0}))},
    {"city", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_note({"Accra", "Tema", "Kumasi"}))},
});

auto out = df.reorder({"city"});
Expected output¶
city    id  sales
Accra   1   100.0
Tema    2   120.0
Kumasi  3    90.0

Example 2. Move selected columns to the front, back, or around an anchor while preserving the rest.

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"id", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({1, 2, 3}))},
    {"sales", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({100.0, 120.0, 90.0}))},
    {"city", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_note({"Accra", "Tema", "Kumasi"}))},
});

auto spec = pluss::table::DataFrame::ReorderSpec::move("sales").after("city");
auto out = df.reorder(spec);
Expected output¶
id  city    sales
1   Accra   100.0
2   Tema    120.0
3   Kumasi   90.0

Example 3. Apply a reusable multi-step reorder plan stored in a standard container.

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"id", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({1, 2, 3}))},
    {"sales", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({100.0, 120.0, 90.0}))},
    {"city", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_note({"Accra", "Tema", "Kumasi"}))},
});

using Move = pluss::table::DataFrame::ReorderSpec;
std::vector<Move> plan{
    Move::move({"city", "sales"}).first(),
    Move::move("id").after("sales"),
};
auto out = df.reorder(plan);
Expected output¶
city    sales  id
Accra   100.0  1
Tema    120.0  2
Kumasi  90.0   3

Example 4. Apply an inline multi-step reorder plan that moves only the columns you care about.

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"col_1", pluss::make_series({1.0, 101.0})},
    {"col_2", pluss::make_series({2.0, 102.0})},
    {"col_3", pluss::make_series({3.0, 103.0})},
    {"col_4", pluss::make_series({4.0, 104.0})},
    {"col_5", pluss::make_series({5.0, 105.0})},
    {"col_6", pluss::make_series({6.0, 106.0})},
    {"col_7", pluss::make_series({7.0, 107.0})},
    {"col_8", pluss::make_series({8.0, 108.0})},
    {"col_9", pluss::make_series({9.0, 109.0})},
    {"col_10", pluss::make_series({10.0, 110.0})},
    {"col_15", pluss::make_series({15.0, 115.0})},
    {"col_16", pluss::make_series({16.0, 116.0})},
    {"col_17", pluss::make_series({17.0, 117.0})},
    {"col_20", pluss::make_series({20.0, 120.0})},
    {"col_21", pluss::make_series({21.0, 121.0})},
    {"col_22", pluss::make_series({22.0, 122.0})},
    {"col_23", pluss::make_series({23.0, 123.0})},
    {"col_24", pluss::make_series({24.0, 124.0})},
    {"col_25", pluss::make_series({25.0, 125.0})},
});

using Move = pluss::table::DataFrame::ReorderSpec;
auto out = df.reorder({
    Move::move({"col_25", "col_10"}).first(),
    Move::move("col_20").before("col_5"),
    Move::move({"col_15", "col_16", "col_17"}).after("col_8"),
    Move::move_regex("^col_2[1-4]$").last(),
});
Expected output¶
out.feature_names():
["col_25", "col_10", "col_1", "col_2", "col_3", "col_4", "col_20", "col_5", "col_6", "col_7", "col_8", "col_15", "col_16", "col_17", "col_9", "col_21", "col_22", "col_23", "col_24"]

out.head():
col_25  col_10  col_1  col_2  col_3  col_4  col_20  col_5  col_6  col_7  col_8  col_15  col_16  col_17  col_9  col_21  col_22  col_23  col_24
25.0    10.0    1.0    2.0    3.0    4.0    20.0    5.0    6.0    7.0    8.0    15.0    16.0    17.0    9.0    21.0    22.0    23.0    24.0
125.0   110.0   101.0  102.0  103.0  104.0  120.0   105.0  106.0  107.0  108.0  115.0   116.0   117.0   109.0  121.0   122.0   123.0   124.0

Practical Behavior¶

  • reorder({"a", "b"}) now means “move these features together and preserve the relative order of everything else.”

  • Use ReorderSpec when you need to move a subset to the front, back, before an anchor, or after an anchor.

  • Use the multi-spec overload when you want to apply several moves in one call from left to right.

  • This avoids listing a 3000-feature schema just to reposition two columns.

repeated_cases¶

API Signature¶

DataFrame::repeated_cases(features: pluss::RangeView<std::string_view> = {}) -> pluss::Series

Notes¶

Returns the rows whose current case labels are duplicates of an earlier row.

Inputs¶

features : pluss::RangeView<std::string_view> Feature name(s) that select the target DataFrame columns for the operation.

pluss::Series Value produced by this call.

Options¶

Option and enum values, when present, are listed with their effects under Inputs.

Examples¶

Example 1. Work with a selected feature subset.

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"id", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({1, 2, 3}))},
    {"sales", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({100.0, 120.0, 90.0}))},
    {"city", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_note({"Accra", "Tema", "Kumasi"}))},
});

auto dup = df.with_cases(pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_note({"cs0", "cs0", "cs2"})));
auto out = dup.repeated_cases();

DataFrame::replace(from: std::string_view, to: std::string_view, features: pluss::RangeView<std::string_view> = {}) -> DataFrame

Notes¶

Replaces matched scalar or pluss-typed values across selected compatible features and returns the updated frame.

Inputs¶

from : const char* Value to search for inside the selected compatible features. Its type decides which feature kinds participate.

to : const char* Replacement value written anywhere from matches. Use pluss::null when you want matched cells to become missing.

features : pluss::RangeView<std::string_view> Optional feature subset. Leave empty to apply the replacement across every compatible feature of the relevant kind.

Output¶

DataFrame Value produced by this call.

Options¶

Option and enum values, when present, are listed with their effects under Inputs.

Examples¶

Example 1. Work with a selected feature subset.

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"midterm_1", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({0.0, 12.0, 0.0}))},
    {"midterm_2", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({8.0, 0.0, 15.0}))},
    {"city", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_note({"Accra", "Tema", "Tema"}))},
});

auto out = df.replace("Tema", "Tamale", {"city"});
Expected output¶
midterm_1  midterm_2  city
0.0        8.0        Accra
12.0       0.0        Tamale
0.0        15.0       Tamale

    {"city", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_note({"Accra", "Tema", "Tema"}))},
});

Expected output¶

5.0        15.0       Tema

Example 21. Work with a selected feature subset.

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"midterm_1", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({0.0, 12.0, 0.0}))},
    {"midterm_2", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({8.0, 0.0, 15.0}))},
    {"city", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_note({"Accra", "Tema", "Tema"}))},
});

Expected output¶
midterm_1  midterm_2  city
0.0        8.0        Accra
12.0       0.0        Tamale
0.0        15.0       Tamale

Practical Behavior¶

  • replace(from, to, features) dispatches by value type, so numeric replacements touch numeric series features while string replacements touch note features.

  • If features is empty, every compatible feature of the relevant kind participates automatically.

  • Use pluss::null as to when you want matched cells to become missing.

resample¶

API Signature¶

DataFrame::resample(time_feature: std::string_view, value_features: pluss::RangeView<std::string_view>, freq: std::string_view, op: std::string_view = "mean", step: std::int64_t = 1, render: bool = true) -> DataFrameView

Notes¶

This is part of the time-aware surface and expects timeline or time-index semantics.

Inputs¶

time_feature : std::string_view Name of the Timeline or TimeIndex feature that defines the resampling, alignment, or calendar axis.

value_features : pluss::RangeView<std::string_view> Feature name(s) to aggregate inside each resampling bin. Leave empty when you want PlussMic to infer compatible value features.

freq : std::string_view Bin or calendar frequency such as "1h", "D", "W", or "M".

op : std::string_view Bin reduction to compute in each time bucket.

Supported values:
- `count`: Count observed values within each bucket.
- `size`: Count rows within each bucket, including missing values.
- `sum`: Compute the numeric sum within each bucket.
- `mean`: Compute the arithmetic mean within each bucket.
- `min`: Compute the minimum within each bucket.
- `max`: Compute the maximum within each bucket.
- `first`: Take the first observed value within each bucket.
- `last`: Take the last observed value within each bucket.

step : std::int64_t Positive frequency multiplier. For example, 6 with hourly frequency means six-hour bins.

render : bool When true, the returned view can auto-render in temporary terminal contexts. Pass false when you want explicit output control.

Output¶

DataFrameView Value produced by this call.

Options¶

Option and enum values, when present, are listed with their effects under Inputs.

Examples¶

Example 1. Choose whether the returned object should auto-render in display contexts.

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"ts", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_timeline({
        "2024-01-01T09:10:00Z",
        "2024-01-01T09:40:00Z",
        "2024-01-01T10:05:00Z",
    }))},
    {"load", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({10.0, 20.0, 15.0}))},
});

auto out = df.resample("ts", {"load"}, "1h", "mean", 1, false);
Expected output¶
ts                   load
2024-01-01T09:00:00Z  15.0
2024-01-01T10:00:00Z  15.0

Practical Behavior¶

  • resample(...) groups rows into temporal bins and aggregates one value per bin and selected feature.

  • count ignores missing values, while size counts rows whether the value is missing or not.

  • For fixed frequencies, bins are anchored from the start of the local day rather than from the first observation timestamp.

  • Numeric reductions such as mean, sum, min, max, first, and last require numeric Series features.

DataFrame::reset_cases(case_feature: std::string = "case") -> DataFrame

Notes¶

Materializes the current case axis as a normal feature, then restores the default positional cases 0..n-1.

    {"id", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({1, 2, 3}))},
    {"sales", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({100.0, 120.0, 90.0}))},

});

auto out = with_cases.reset_cases("case");

reshuffle¶

API Signature¶

DataFrame::reshuffle(axis: int = 0, random_state: std::optional<std::uint64_t> = std::nullopt) -> DataFrame

Notes¶

Use this method through the public contract shown above.

Inputs¶

axis : int Shuffle axis. Use 0 to permute rows and 1 to permute feature order.

random_state : std::optional<std::uint64_t> Deterministic seed for reproducible row or feature shuffles.

Output¶

DataFrame Value produced by this call.

Options¶

Option and enum values, when present, are listed with their effects under Inputs.

Examples¶

Example 1. Shuffle rows or features depending on the selected axis.

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"id", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({1, 2, 3}))},
    {"sales", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({100.0, 120.0, 90.0}))},
    {"city", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_note({"Accra", "Tema", "Kumasi"}))},
});

auto rows = df.reshuffle(0, 7);
auto cols = df.reshuffle(1, 7);
Expected output¶
rows.head():
id  sales  city
3    90.0  Kumasi
1   100.0  Accra
2   120.0  Tema

cols.head():
city    id  sales
Accra   1   100.0
Tema    2   120.0
Kumasi  3    90.0

Practical Behavior¶

  • reshuffle(axis=0) permutes rows and keeps the feature order unchanged.

  • reshuffle(axis=1) permutes feature order and keeps the row order unchanged.

  • Pass random_state when you need deterministic shuffling for docs, tests, or reproducible data splits.

rolling¶

API Signature¶

DataFrame::rolling(specs: pluss::RangeView<WindowSpec>, keep_input: bool = true) -> DataFrame

Notes¶

Computes rolling-window features and returns them as a derived frame.

Inputs¶

specs : pluss::RangeView<WindowSpec> Window specs that define the output name, source feature, rolling operation, window width, and minimum observation policy.

keep_input : bool When true, the original features stay in the output and rolling features are appended. When false, only the derived rolling outputs are returned.

Output¶

DataFrame Value produced by this call.

Options¶

Option and enum values, when present, are listed with their effects under Inputs.

Examples¶

Example 1. Use this overload when its parameter combination matches the result shape or control level you need.

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"id", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({1, 2, 3}))},
    {"sales", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({100.0, 120.0, 90.0}))},
    {"city", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_note({"Accra", "Tema", "Kumasi"}))},
});

auto out = df.rolling({{.output = "sales_roll", .feature = "sales", .op = pluss::table::ThreadWindowOp::RollingMean, .window = 2, .min_periods = 1}}, false);
Expected output¶
sales_roll
100.0
110.0
105.0

Practical Behavior¶

  • rolling(...) is the frame-level window-engineering route, so one call can derive several rolling outputs at once.

  • keep_input=true appends rolling outputs to the original frame, while keep_input=false returns only the engineered outputs.

  • Each WindowSpec controls the output name, source feature, operation, window width, and minimum observation rule.

sample¶

API Signatures¶

DataFrame::sample(frac: Float) -> template <class Float> requires std::floating_point<Float> DataFrame

DataFrame::sample(frac: Float, random_state: std::uint64_t, replace: bool = false, axis: int = 0) -> template <class Float> requires std::floating_point<Float> DataFrame

DataFrame::sample(frac: Float, replace: bool, axis: int) -> template <class Float> requires std::floating_point<Float> DataFrame

DataFrame::sample(n: std::int64_t) -> DataFrame

DataFrame::sample(n: std::int64_t, random_state: std::uint64_t, replace: bool = false, axis: int = 0) -> DataFrame

DataFrame::sample(n: std::int64_t, replace: bool, axis: int) -> DataFrame

Notes¶

Returns a random sample of rows.

Inputs¶

frac : Float Fraction of the selected axis to draw. Values above 1.0 require replace=true.

random_state : std::uint64_t Deterministic seed for reproducible sampling and shuffling.

replace : bool When true, the same row may be drawn more than once. Feature sampling currently requires replace=false.

axis : int Sampling axis. Use 0 for rows and 1 for features.

n : std::int64_t Number of rows or features to draw from the selected axis.

Output¶

DataFrame Value produced by this call.

Options¶

Option and enum values, when present, are listed with their effects under Inputs.

Examples¶

Example 1. Sample a fraction of the selected axis without an explicit random seed.

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"id", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({1, 2, 3}))},
    {"sales", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({100.0, 120.0, 90.0}))},
    {"city", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_note({"Accra", "Tema", "Kumasi"}))},
});

auto out = df.sample(0.67, false, 0);
Expected output¶
id  sales  city
1   100.0  Accra
3    90.0  Kumasi

Example 2. Sample a fraction of the selected axis with an explicit random seed.

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"id", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({1, 2, 3}))},
    {"sales", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({100.0, 120.0, 90.0}))},
    {"city", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_note({"Accra", "Tema", "Kumasi"}))},
});

auto out = df.sample(0.67, 7, false, 0);
Expected output¶
id  sales  city
1   100.0  Accra
3    90.0  Kumasi

Example 3. Sample a fraction of the selected axis without an explicit random seed.

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"id", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({1, 2, 3}))},
    {"sales", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({100.0, 120.0, 90.0}))},
    {"city", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_note({"Accra", "Tema", "Kumasi"}))},
});

auto out = df.sample(0.67, false, 0);
Expected output¶
id  sales  city
1   100.0  Accra
3    90.0  Kumasi

Example 4. Sample rows with the default settings.

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"id", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({1, 2, 3}))},
    {"sales", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({100.0, 120.0, 90.0}))},
    {"city", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_note({"Accra", "Tema", "Kumasi"}))},
});

auto out = df.sample(2);
Expected output¶
id  sales  city
1   100.0  Accra
3    90.0  Kumasi

Example 5. Sample rows or features with an explicit random seed.

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"id", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({1, 2, 3}))},
    {"sales", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({100.0, 120.0, 90.0}))},
    {"city", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_note({"Accra", "Tema", "Kumasi"}))},
});

auto rows = df.sample(2, 7, false, 0);
auto cols = df.sample(2, 7, false, 1);
Expected output¶
rows.head():
id  sales  city
1   100.0  Accra
3    90.0  Kumasi

cols.head():
sales  city
100.0  Accra
120.0  Tema
90.0   Kumasi

Example 6. Sample rows or features while controlling replacement and axis directly.

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"id", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({1, 2, 3}))},
    {"sales", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({100.0, 120.0, 90.0}))},
    {"city", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_note({"Accra", "Tema", "Kumasi"}))},
});

auto rows = df.sample(2, false, 0);
auto cols = df.sample(2, false, 1);
Expected output¶
rows.head():
id  sales  city
1   100.0  Accra
3    90.0  Kumasi

cols.head():
sales  city
100.0  Accra
120.0  Tema
90.0   Kumasi

Practical Behavior¶

  • sample(n, ...) draws a fixed number of rows by default, or features when axis=1.

  • sample(frac, ...) draws a proportion of the selected axis.

  • replace=true enables sampling with replacement. For frac > 1, replacement is required.

save_as¶

API Signatures¶

DataFrame::save_as(target_type: std::string_view, filepath: std::string_view, config: const pluss::loader::Config& = {}) -> void

DataFrame::save_as(target_type: std::string_view, filepath: std::string_view, config_entries: std::initializer_list<pluss::loader::ConfigEntry>) -> void

Notes¶

Writes the frame using the explicitly supplied output format selector rather than a dedicated saver overload.

Inputs¶

target_type : std::string_view Format or target selector string used by this overload.

filepath : std::string_view File location to read from or write to. Use a neutral project path such as path/to/data.csv.

config : const pluss::loader::Config& Loader or saver configuration object. Use this when you want to pass a prebuilt option bundle instead of positional arguments.

Notes¶

Writes the frame to CSV. Set add_cases=true when you want the current case axis exported as a regular column so row labels survive the round trip.

Inputs¶

filepath : std::string_view File location to read from or write to. Use a neutral project path such as path/to/data.csv.

add_cases : bool When true, the current case axis is exported as its own column so row labels can be reconstructed when the file is loaded again.

header : bool Controls whether feature names are written to, or expected from, the file header row.

sep : char Column separator used for delimited text files such as CSV.

na_rep : std::string String written anywhere a null or missing value must be serialized.

case_label : std::optional<std::string> Optional column label to use for the exported case axis when add_cases=true.

float_format : std::optional<std::string> Optional numeric formatting string used when floating-point values are written to text output.

quotechar : char Quote character used when writing delimited text output.

doublequote : bool When true, embedded quote characters are escaped by doubling them in CSV-style output.

line_terminator : std::string Line ending written between serialized rows in text-based export.

decimal : char Decimal marker used when formatting floating-point output.

encoding : std::string Text encoding used when reading or writing text-based files.

config : const pluss::loader::Config& Loader or saver configuration object. Use this when you want to pass a prebuilt option bundle instead of positional arguments.

config_entries : std::initializer_list<pluss::loader::ConfigEntry> Inline configuration entries used to build a lightweight loader configuration without naming a separate config object.

options : const pluss::loader::WriteCsvOptions& Typed loader, renderer, SQL, plotting, or policy options for this overload.

select_like¶

API Signature¶

DataFrame::select_like(needle: std::string_view, case_sensitive: bool = true) -> DataFrame

Notes¶

Selects only the features whose names contain the requested substring.

Inputs¶

needle : std::string_view Substring token used to match feature names.

case_sensitive : bool When true, substring matching respects letter case. When false, feature names are matched case-insensitively.

Output¶

DataFrame Value produced by this call.

Options¶

Option and enum values, when present, are listed with their effects under Inputs.

Examples¶

Example 1. Use this overload when its parameter combination matches the result shape or control level you need.

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"midterm_1", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({70.0, 80.0, 90.0}))},
    {"midterm_2", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({75.0, 85.0, 95.0}))},
    {"final_points", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({88.0, 91.0, 94.0}))},
    {"city", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_note({"Accra", "Tema", "Kumasi"}))},
});

auto out = df.select_like("midterm");
Expected output¶
midterm_1  midterm_2
70.0       75.0
80.0       85.0
90.0       95.0

Practical Behavior¶

  • select_like(...) filters feature names, not row values.

  • The output keeps the original row order and case axis unchanged.

  • Use this when you want schema-driven feature selection without listing every matching feature manually.

DataFrame::set_axis(feature_names: pluss::RangeView<std::string_view>) -> DataFrame

Notes¶

Replaces the full feature label set with the supplied names in positional order.

Inputs¶

feature_names : pluss::RangeView<std::string_view> Full replacement feature-label list in final left-to-right order. The count must match the current number of features.

Output¶

DataFrame Value produced by this call.

Options¶

Option and enum values, when present, are listed with their effects under Inputs.

Examples¶

Example 1. Use this overload when its parameter combination matches the result shape or control level you need.

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"id", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({1, 2, 3}))},
    {"sales", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({100.0, 120.0, 90.0}))},
    {"city", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_note({"Accra", "Tema", "Kumasi"}))},
});

auto out = df.set_axis({"revenue", "location", "id_new"});
Expected output¶
revenue  location  id_new
100.0    Accra     1
120.0    Tema      2
90.0     Kumasi    3

set_cases¶

API Signature¶

DataFrame::set_cases(feature_name: std::string_view, drop_feature: bool = true) -> DataFrame

Notes¶

Promotes one feature to become the case axis. With the default drop_feature=true, that feature stops being a normal column and becomes the row labels instead.

Inputs¶

feature_name : std::string_view Name of the target feature to read, rewrite, sort by, or promote to cases.

drop_feature : bool When true, the feature promoted to cases is removed from the ordinary feature columns.

Output¶

DataFrame Value produced by this call.

Options¶

Option and enum values, when present, are listed with their effects under Inputs.

Examples¶

Example 1. Work with one named feature.

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"id", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({1, 2, 3}))},
    {"sales", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({100.0, 120.0, 90.0}))},
    {"city", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_note({"Accra", "Tema", "Kumasi"}))},
});

auto out = df.set_cases("city");
Expected output¶
df.head():
id  sales  city
1   100.0  Accra
2   120.0  Tema
3    90.0  Kumasi

out.cases():
["Accra", "Tema", "Kumasi"]

out.head():
id  sales
1   100.0
2   120.0
3    90.0

set_features¶

API Signatures¶

DataFrame::set_features(name: std::string_view, value: const Thread&) -> DataFrame

DataFrame::set_features(names: pluss::RangeView<std::string_view>, values: pluss::RangeView<Thread>) -> DataFrame

Notes¶

Returns a new frame with one added or replaced feature.

Inputs¶

name : std::string_view Name used to identify the target object, field, feature, or slot for this overload.

value : const Thread& Replacement, fill, or write value used by mutation-style methods such as put(...), fillna(...), or replace(...).

names : pluss::RangeView<std::string_view> Collection of feature, slot, or stream names supplied in positional order.

values : pluss::RangeView<Thread> Value collection supplied to this overload. The ordering must match the corresponding names or positions expected by the method.

Output¶

DataFrame Value produced by this call.

Options¶

Option and enum values, when present, are listed with their effects under Inputs.

Examples¶

Example 1. Add or replace one column by name.

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"id", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({1, 2, 3}))},
    {"sales", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({100.0, 120.0, 90.0}))},
    {"city", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_note({"Accra", "Tema", "Kumasi"}))},
});

auto out = df.set_features("profit", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({40.0, 35.0, 30.0})));
Expected output¶

2   120.0  Tema    35.0
3    90.0  Kumasi  30.0

Example 2. Add or replace several columns in one call.

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"id", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({1, 2, 3}))},
    {"sales", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({100.0, 120.0, 90.0}))},
    {"city", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_note({"Accra", "Tema", "Kumasi"}))},
});

auto out = df.set_features(
    {"profit", "cost"},
    {
        pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({40.0, 35.0, 30.0})),
        pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({60.0, 85.0, 60.0})),
    });
Expected output¶
id  sales  city    profit
1   100.0  Accra   40.0
2   120.0  Tema    35.0
3    90.0  Kumasi  30.0

shift¶

API Signatures¶

DataFrame::shift(features: pluss::RangeView<std::string_view>, periods: std::int64_t = 1) -> DataFrame

DataFrame::shift(periods: std::int64_t = 1) -> DataFrame

Notes¶

Use this method through the public contract shown above.

Inputs¶

features : pluss::RangeView<std::string_view> Feature name(s) that select the target DataFrame columns for the operation.

periods : std::int64_t Number of rows to shift selected feature values. Positive values move values downward and introduce missing entries at the top; negative values move upward.

Output¶

DataFrame Value produced by this call.

Options¶

Option and enum values, when present, are listed with their effects under Inputs.

Examples¶

Example 1. Shift only selected columns by a fixed number of rows.

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"id", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({1, 2, 3}))},
    {"sales", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({100.0, 120.0, 90.0}))},
    {"city", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_note({"Accra", "Tema", "Kumasi"}))},
});

auto out = df.shift({"sales"}, 2);
Expected output¶
id  sales  city
1   100.0  Accra
2   120.0  Tema
3    90.0  Kumasi

Example 2. Shift every compatible column by a fixed number of rows.

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"id", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({1, 2, 3}))},
    {"sales", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({100.0, 120.0, 90.0}))},
    {"city", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_note({"Accra", "Tema", "Kumasi"}))},
});

auto out = df.shift(2);
Expected output¶
id  sales  city
1   100.0  Accra
2   120.0  Tema
3    90.0  Kumasi

shift_time¶

API Signature¶

DataFrame::shift_time(features: pluss::RangeView<std::string_view>, periods: int, freq: std::string_view) -> DataFrame

Notes¶

This is part of the time-aware surface and expects timeline or time-index semantics.

Inputs¶

features : pluss::RangeView<std::string_view> Feature name(s) that select the target DataFrame columns for the operation.

periods : int Number of row or time steps to shift forward or backward. Positive values usually move data down or later; negative values move it up or earlier.

freq : std::string_view Bin or calendar frequency such as "1h", "D", "W", or "M".

Output¶

DataFrame Value produced by this call.

Options¶

Option and enum values, when present, are listed with their effects under Inputs.

Examples¶

Example 1. Work with a selected feature subset.

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"ts", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_timeline({
        "2024-01-01T09:10:00Z",
        "2024-01-01T09:40:00Z",
        "2024-01-01T10:05:00Z",
    }))},
    {"load", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({10.0, 20.0, 15.0}))},
});

auto out = df.shift_time({"ts"}, 1, "hour");
Expected output¶
ts
2024-01-01T10:10:00Z
2024-01-01T10:40:00Z
2024-01-01T11:05:00Z

shuffle¶

API Signature¶

DataFrame::shuffle(random_state: std::optional<std::uint64_t> = std::nullopt) -> DataFrame

Notes¶

Use this method through the public contract shown above.

Inputs¶

random_state : std::optional<std::uint64_t> Deterministic seed for reproducible row shuffles.

Output¶

DataFrame Value produced by this call.

Options¶

Option and enum values, when present, are listed with their effects under Inputs.

Examples¶

Example 1. Shuffle row order while keeping the feature order unchanged.

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"id", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({1, 2, 3}))},
    {"sales", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({100.0, 120.0, 90.0}))},
    {"city", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_note({"Accra", "Tema", "Kumasi"}))},
});

auto out = df.shuffle(7);
Expected output¶
id  sales  city
3    90.0  Kumasi
1   100.0  Accra
2   120.0  Tema

Practical Behavior¶

  • shuffle(random_state) is the row-order helper for the common case where you want to permute rows and leave the feature order alone.

  • It is equivalent to reshuffle(axis=0, ...), but reads more directly in train/test split and stochastic preview workflows.

sort_cases¶

API Signature¶

DataFrame::sort_cases(ascending: bool = true, nulls_last: bool = true) -> DataFrame

Notes¶

Sorts rows by the current case axis rather than by a data feature.

Inputs¶

ascending : bool When true, case labels are sorted ascending. When false, they are sorted descending.

nulls_last : bool When true, null case labels are placed after observed labels. When false, they are placed first.

Output¶

DataFrame Value produced by this call.

Options¶

Option and enum values, when present, are listed with their effects under Inputs.

Examples¶

Example 1. Use this overload when its parameter combination matches the result shape or control level you need.

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"id", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({1, 2, 3}))},
    {"sales", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({100.0, 120.0, 90.0}))},
    {"city", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_note({"Accra", "Tema", "Kumasi"}))},
});

auto with_cases = df.with_cases(pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_note({"cs2", "cs0", "cs1"})));
auto out = with_cases.sort_cases(true, true);
Expected output¶
with_cases.cases():
["cs2", "cs0", "cs1"]

out.cases():
["cs0", "cs1", "cs2"]

out.head():
id  sales  city
2   120.0  Tema
3    90.0  Kumasi
1   100.0  Accra

sort_values¶

API Signatures¶

DataFrame::sort_values(features: pluss::RangeView<std::string_view>, ascending: bool = true, nulls_last: bool = true) -> DataFrame

DataFrame::sort_values(specs: pluss::RangeView<ArrangeSpec>) -> DataFrame

Notes¶

Reorders rows using one or more feature values as sort keys.

Inputs¶

features : pluss::RangeView<std::string_view> Feature names used as sort keys when you want the same ascending/null policy for every key.

ascending : bool When you use the simple feature-list overload, this one switch applies to every sort key. true sorts ascending and false sorts descending.

nulls_last : bool When true, null values are placed after observed values for every sort key in the simple overload. When false, nulls are placed first.

specs : pluss::RangeView<ArrangeSpec> Collection of structured operation specs. Each element describes one requested summary, derive, transform, group, or placement rule depending on the method.

Output¶

DataFrame Value produced by this call.

Options¶

Option and enum values, when present, are listed with their effects under Inputs.

Examples¶

Example 1. Sort rows using one shared ascending and null-order policy for every selected sort key.

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"id", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({1, 2, 3}))},
    {"sales", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({100.0, 120.0, 90.0}))},
    {"city", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_note({"Accra", "Tema", "Kumasi"}))},
});

auto out = df.sort_values({"sales"}, false, true);
Expected output¶
id  sales  city
2   120.0  Tema
1   100.0  Accra
3    90.0  Kumasi

Example 2. Sort rows using explicit per-column sort specifications.

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"id", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({1, 2, 3}))},
    {"sales", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({100.0, 120.0, 90.0}))},
    {"city", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_note({"Accra", "Tema", "Kumasi"}))},
});

auto out = df.sort_values({{.feature = "sales", .ascending = false}});
Expected output¶
id  sales  city
2   120.0  Tema
1   100.0  Accra
3    90.0  Kumasi

sql¶

API Signatures¶

DataFrame::sql() -> DataFrameSqlAccessor

DataFrame::sql(options: SqlOptions) -> DataFrameSqlAccessor

Notes¶

Use this when the transformation is easier to express as SQL than as a chained sequence of table verbs.

Inputs¶

options : SqlOptions SQL execution options such as engine or binding policy for the returned SQL accessor.

Output¶

DataFrameSqlAccessor Value produced by this call.

Options¶

Option and enum values, when present, are listed with their effects under Inputs.

Examples¶

Example 1. Create the SQL accessor with default options and run a query immediately.

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"id", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({1, 2, 3}))},
    {"sales", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({100.0, 120.0, 90.0}))},
    {"city", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_note({"Accra", "Tema", "Kumasi"}))},
});

auto out = df.sql().execute("SELECT id, sales FROM self WHERE sales > 95");
Expected output¶
id  sales
1   100.0
2   120.0

Example 2. Create the SQL accessor with an explicit SQL options object before running a query.

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"id", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({1, 2, 3}))},
    {"sales", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({100.0, 120.0, 90.0}))},
    {"city", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_note({"Accra", "Tema", "Kumasi"}))},
});

pluss::table::DataFrame::SqlOptions options;
auto sql = df.sql(options);
auto out = sql.execute("SELECT id, sales FROM self WHERE sales > 95");
Expected output¶
id  sales
1   100.0
2   120.0

Practical Behavior¶

  • sql() returns the SQL accessor; it does not execute a statement by itself.

  • Call .execute(...) on the accessor when you want a result frame immediately.

  • Use prepare_sql(...) when the same query will be executed repeatedly with changing bindings.

std¶

API Signatures¶

DataFrame::std(axis: int, skipna: bool = true) -> Thread

DataFrame::std(axis: std::int64_t, skipna: bool = true) -> Thread

DataFrame::std(render: bool = true) -> DataFrameView

Notes¶

Computes per-feature standard deviations for the selected numeric features.

Inputs¶

axis : int Axis selector. On DataFrame, 0 usually means rows/cases and 1 means features/columns.

skipna : bool When true, missing values are skipped during the reduction. When false, missing state can affect the result.

render : bool When true, the returned view can auto-render in temporary terminal contexts. Pass false when you want explicit output control.

Output¶

Thread Value produced by this call.

DataFrameView Value produced by this call.

Options¶

Option and enum values, when present, are listed with their effects under Inputs.

Examples¶

Example 1. Compute std across rows instead of returning one summary value per numeric column.

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"a", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({1.0, 2.0, 3.0}))},
    {"b", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({2.0, 4.0, 5.0}))},
});

auto out = df.std(1, true);
Expected output¶
feature  value
id       1.0
sales    15.275252317

Example 2. Compute std across rows instead of returning one summary value per numeric column.

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"a", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({1.0, 2.0, 3.0}))},
    {"b", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({2.0, 4.0, 5.0}))},
});

auto out = df.std(static_cast<std::int64_t>(1), true);
Expected output¶
feature  value
id       1.0
sales    15.275252317

Example 3. Compute std for each numeric column in the frame.

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"id", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({1, 2, 3}))},
    {"sales", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({100.0, 120.0, 90.0}))},
    {"city", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_note({"Accra", "Tema", "Kumasi"}))},
});

auto out = df.std(false);
Expected output¶
feature  value
id       1.0
sales    15.275252317

Practical Behavior¶

  • std(...) reduces the selected numeric features to one summary row.

  • Non-numeric features are skipped rather than coerced.

  • The output stays in DataFrame form, which makes these reducers easy to reuse in downstream frame pipelines.

stitch_on¶

API Signatures¶

DataFrame::stitch_on(left_feature: std::string_view, right: const DataFrame&, right_feature: std::string_view = "", right_suffix: std::string = "_right") -> DataFrame

DataFrame::stitch_on(left_features: pluss::RangeView<std::string_view>, right: const DataFrame&, right_features: pluss::RangeView<std::string_view> = {}, right_suffix: std::string = "_right") -> DataFrame

DataFrame::stitch_on(left_features: std::initializer_list<std::string_view>, right: const DataFrame&, right_features: std::initializer_list<std::string_view> = {}, right_suffix: std::string = "_right") -> DataFrame

Notes¶

Matches rows from two frames using key features and appends the matched features from the right-hand frame.

Inputs¶

left_feature : std::string_view Key feature on the left frame used to match rows against the right frame.

right : const DataFrame& When true, intervals are right-closed. When false, they are left-closed and right-open.

right_feature : std::string_view Matching key feature on the right frame. Leave empty to reuse the left feature name.

right_suffix : std::string Suffix added to right-hand feature names only when a non-key right feature would otherwise collide with an existing left feature name.

left_features : pluss::RangeView<std::string_view> Key features on the left frame used to build a composite match key against the right frame.

right_features : pluss::RangeView<std::string_view> Matching key features on the right frame. Leave empty to reuse the left feature names in the same order.

Output¶

DataFrame Value produced by this call.

Options¶

Option and enum values, when present, are listed with their effects under Inputs.

Examples¶

Example 1. Attach right-hand features by matching on one key feature.

auto left = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"id", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({1, 2, 3}))},
    {"sales", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({100.0, 120.0, 90.0}))},
});
auto right = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"id", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({1, 2, 3}))},
    {"cost", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({60.0, 80.0, 55.0}))},
});

auto out = left.stitch_on("id", right, "id", "_right");
Expected output¶
id  sales  cost
1   100.0  60.0
2   120.0  80.0
3    90.0  55.0

Example 2. Attach right-hand features by matching on one key feature.

});

});

sub¶

API Signatures¶

DataFrame::sub(other: const DataFrame&) -> DataFrame

DataFrame::sub(other: double) -> DataFrame

Notes¶

This applies arithmetic across the compatible numeric payloads in the current object.

Inputs¶

other : const DataFrame& Second frame, thread, or scalar operand supplied for binary combination, comparison, alignment, or join-style work.

Output¶

DataFrame Value produced by this call.

Options¶

Option and enum values, when present, are listed with their effects under Inputs.

Examples¶

Example 1. Subtract each compatible numeric cell against another aligned frame.

auto left = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"id", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({1, 2, 3}))},
    {"sales", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({100.0, 120.0, 90.0}))},
});
auto right = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"id", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({2, 2, 4}))},
    {"sales", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({110.0, 110.0, 100.0}))},
});

auto out = left.sub(right);
Expected output¶
id  sales  city
1   100.0  Accra
2   120.0  Tema
3    90.0  Kumasi

Example 2. Subtract each compatible numeric cell against one broadcast scalar value.

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"id", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({1, 2, 3}))},
    {"sales", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({100.0, 120.0, 90.0}))},
    {"city", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_note({"Accra", "Tema", "Kumasi"}))},
});

auto out = df.sub(10);
Expected output¶
id  sales  city
-9  90.0   Accra
-8  110.0  Tema
-7  80.0   Kumasi

sum¶

API Signatures¶

DataFrame::sum(axis: int, skipna: bool = true) -> Thread

DataFrame::sum(axis: std::int64_t, skipna: bool = true) -> Thread

DataFrame::sum(render: bool = true) -> DataFrameView

Notes¶

Computes per-feature sums for the selected numeric features.

Inputs¶

axis : int Axis selector. On DataFrame, 0 usually means rows/cases and 1 means features/columns.

skipna : bool When true, missing values are skipped during the reduction. When false, missing state can affect the result.

render : bool When true, the returned view can auto-render in temporary terminal contexts. Pass false when you want explicit output control.

Output¶

Thread Value produced by this call.

DataFrameView Value produced by this call.

Options¶

Option and enum values, when present, are listed with their effects under Inputs.

Examples¶

Example 1. Compute sum across rows instead of returning one summary value per numeric column.

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"a", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({1.0, 2.0, 3.0}))},
    {"b", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({2.0, 4.0, 5.0}))},
});

auto out = df.sum(1, true);
Expected output¶
feature  value
id       6
sales    310.0

Example 2. Compute sum across rows instead of returning one summary value per numeric column.

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"a", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({1.0, 2.0, 3.0}))},
    {"b", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({2.0, 4.0, 5.0}))},
});

auto out = df.sum(static_cast<std::int64_t>(1), true);
Expected output¶
feature  value
id       6
sales    310.0

Example 3. Compute sum for each numeric column in the frame.

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"id", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({1, 2, 3}))},
    {"sales", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({100.0, 120.0, 90.0}))},
    {"city", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_note({"Accra", "Tema", "Kumasi"}))},
});

auto out = df.sum(false);
Expected output¶
feature  value
id       6
sales    310.0

Practical Behavior¶

  • sum(...) reduces the selected numeric features to one summary row.

  • Non-numeric features are skipped rather than coerced.

  • The output stays in DataFrame form, which makes these reducers easy to reuse in downstream frame pipelines.

T¶

tabelize¶

API Signatures¶

DataFrame::tabelize(catalog: const pluss::kindle::Catalog&) -> DataFrame

DataFrame::tabelize(catalog: const pluss::kindle::Catalog&, policy: const pluss::kindle::TabelizePolicy&) -> DataFrame

Notes¶

Converts a Kindle Catalog into a tabular DataFrame, preserving stream alignment as rows.

Inputs¶

catalog : const pluss::kindle::Catalog& Catalog payload supplied to this overload.

policy : const pluss::kindle::TabelizePolicy& Policy object that changes the structural behavior of this overload.

Output¶

DataFrame Value produced by this call.

Options¶

Option and enum values, when present, are listed with their effects under Inputs.

Examples¶

Example 1. Convert a Kindle catalog into a frame with the default tabelization policy.

using namespace pluss::kindle::literals;
auto catalog = pluss::kindle::Catalog({"sales"_k = pluss::kindle::Stream(pluss::make_series({10.0, 20.0, 30.0}))});
auto out = pluss::table::DataFrame::tabelize(catalog);
Expected output¶
sales
10.0
20.0
30.0

Example 2. Convert a Kindle catalog into a frame with an explicit tabelization policy.

using namespace pluss::kindle::literals;
auto catalog = pluss::kindle::Catalog({"sales"_k = pluss::kindle::Stream(pluss::make_series({10.0, 20.0, 30.0}))});
pluss::kindle::TabelizePolicy policy;
auto out = pluss::table::DataFrame::tabelize(catalog, policy);
Expected output¶
sales
10.0
20.0
30.0

Practical Behavior¶

  • tabelize(catalog) is the explicit bridge from Kindle stream collections into the DataFrame model.

  • Aligned streams become DataFrame features, and stream position becomes row position.

  • Use the policy overload when you want explicit tabelization rules instead of the defaults.

tail¶

API Signature¶

DataFrame::tail(n: std::int64_t = 5, render: bool = true) -> DataFrameView

Notes¶

Returns the last n rows of the frame.

Inputs¶

n : std::int64_t Number of trailing rows to keep from the bottom of the frame.

render : bool When true, the returned view can auto-render in temporary terminal contexts. Pass false when you want explicit output control.

Output¶

DataFrameView Value produced by this call.

Options¶

Option and enum values, when present, are listed with their effects under Inputs.

Examples¶

Example 1. Choose whether the returned object should auto-render in display contexts.

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"id", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({1, 2, 3}))},
    {"sales", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({100.0, 120.0, 90.0}))},
    {"city", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_note({"Accra", "Tema", "Kumasi"}))},
});

auto out = df.tail(2, false);
Expected output¶
id  sales  city
2   120.0  Tema
3    90.0  Kumasi

Practical Behavior¶

  • tail(n) preserves the original feature order and returns the last n rows.

  • If n is larger than the frame height, the whole frame is returned.

  • The returned object is a DataFrameView, so it behaves like a lightweight preview slice rather than a deep copy.

tally¶

API Signatures¶

DataFrame::tally(feature: std::string_view, top_n: std::int64_t = 0, dropna: bool = true, render: bool = true) -> DataFrameView

DataFrame::tally(features: pluss::RangeView<std::string_view>, top_n: std::int64_t = 0, dropna: bool = true, render: bool = true) -> DataFrameView

DataFrame::tally(top_n: std::int64_t = 0, dropna: bool = true, render: bool = true) -> DataFrameView

Notes¶

Counts how many rows fall into each distinct value of the grouping feature.

Inputs¶

feature : std::string_view Name of the source feature used by the operation.

top_n : std::int64_t Optional cap on how many grouped rows to keep after sorting. Use 0 to keep every group.

dropna : bool When true, null grouping keys or null values are excluded where the method supports that policy. When false, null participates instead of being removed.

render : bool When true, the returned view can auto-render in temporary terminal contexts. Pass false when you want explicit output control.

features : pluss::RangeView<std::string_view> Feature name(s) that select the target DataFrame columns for the operation.

Output¶

DataFrameView Value produced by this call.

Options¶

Option and enum values, when present, are listed with their effects under Inputs.

Examples¶

Example 1. Count the distinct values in one named feature.

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"city", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_note({"Accra", "Accra", "Tema", "Tema"}))},
    {"product", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_note({"A", "B", "A", "B"}))},
    {"sales", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({100.0, 120.0, 90.0, 150.0}))},
});

auto out = df.tally("city", 3, true, false);
Expected output¶
city    count
Accra   2
Tema    2

Example 2. Count distinct combinations across several features.

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"city", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_note({"Accra", "Accra", "Tema", "Tema"}))},
    {"product", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_note({"A", "B", "A", "B"}))},
    {"sales", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({100.0, 120.0, 90.0, 150.0}))},
});

auto out = df.tally({"city", "product"}, 5, true, false);
Expected output¶
city    count
Accra   2
Tema    2

Example 3. Count distinct row groups using the default tally target.

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"city", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_note({"Accra", "Accra", "Tema", "Tema"}))},
    {"product", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_note({"A", "B", "A", "B"}))},
    {"sales", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({100.0, 120.0, 90.0, 150.0}))},
});

auto out = df.tally(3, true, false);
Expected output¶
city    count
Accra   2
Tema    2

title¶

API Signatures¶

DataFrame::title() -> std::string

DataFrame::title(title: std::string) -> DataFrame

Notes¶

Gets the current frame title or returns a titled copy, depending on the overload.

Inputs¶

title : std::string Human-readable title stamp to attach to the returned frame.

Output¶

std::string Rendered string result.

DataFrame Value produced by this call.

Options¶

Option and enum values, when present, are listed with their effects under Inputs.

Examples¶

Example 1. Return a titled copy of the current frame.

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"id", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({1, 2, 3}))},
    {"sales", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({100.0, 120.0, 90.0}))},
    {"city", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_note({"Accra", "Tema", "Kumasi"}))},
});

auto titled = df.title("sales_report");
auto out = titled.title();
Expected output¶
sales_report

Example 2. Return a titled copy of the current frame.

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"id", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({1, 2, 3}))},
    {"sales", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({100.0, 120.0, 90.0}))},
    {"city", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_note({"Accra", "Tema", "Kumasi"}))},
});

auto out = df.title("sales_report");
Expected output¶
out.title():
sales_report

out.head():
id  sales  city
1   100.0  Accra
2   120.0  Tema
3    90.0  Kumasi

Practical Behavior¶

  • title() with no argument reads the current frame title.

  • title("...") returns a titled copy and leaves the source frame unchanged.

  • title_("...") mutates the current frame title in place.

top¶

API Signature¶

DataFrame::top(feature: std::string_view, n: std::int64_t) -> DataFrame

Notes¶

Returns the rows with the largest values in the selected feature.

Inputs¶

feature : std::string_view Name of the source feature used by the operation.

n : std::int64_t Number of rows, entries, or depth items to keep in the preview.

Output¶

DataFrame Value produced by this call.

Options¶

Option and enum values, when present, are listed with their effects under Inputs.

Examples¶

Example 1. Work with one named feature.

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"id", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({1, 2, 3}))},
    {"sales", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({100.0, 120.0, 90.0}))},
    {"city", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_note({"Accra", "Tema", "Kumasi"}))},
});

auto out = df.top("sales", 2);
Expected output¶
id  sales  city
2   120.0  Tema
1   100.0  Accra

Practical Behavior¶

  • top(feature, n) sorts descending by the selected feature, keeps nulls last, then returns the first n rows.

  • The output rows stay aligned across every feature; this is not a single-column extraction.

  • Use bottom(...) when you want the smallest rows instead of the largest ones.

transform¶

API Signatures¶

DataFrame::transform(feature: std::string_view, fn: const std::function<Thread(const DataFrame&)>&) -> DataFrame

DataFrame::transform(feature: std::string_view, fn: const std::function<Thread(const Thread&)>&) -> DataFrame

DataFrame::transform(fn: const std::function<Thread(const Thread&)>&) -> DataFrame

DataFrame::transform(specs: pluss::RangeView<TransformSpec>) -> DataFrame

Notes¶

Rewrites one feature, several features, or all features by applying a user function to each targeted thread.

Inputs¶

feature : std::string_view Target feature name to rewrite, or output feature name when you use the frame-aware derive overload.

fn : const std::function<Thread(const DataFrame&)>& Thread-to-thread or frame-to-thread transform function, depending on the overload. The returned thread must match the frame case count.

specs : pluss::RangeView<TransformSpec> Collection of structured operation specs. Each element describes one requested summary, derive, transform, group, or placement rule depending on the method.

Output¶

DataFrame Value produced by this call.

Options¶

Option and enum values, when present, are listed with their effects under Inputs.

Examples¶

Example 1. Derive or replace one feature by computing it from the full frame.

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"id", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({1, 2, 3}))},
    {"sales", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({100.0, 120.0, 90.0}))},
    {"city", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_note({"Accra", "Tema", "Kumasi"}))},
});

auto out = df.transform("sales_plus_10", [](const pluss::table::DataFrame& frame) { return pluss::table::Thread(frame.features("sales").as_series().add(10.0)); });
Expected output¶
id  sales  city    sales_plus_10
1   100.0  Accra   110.0
2   120.0  Tema    130.0
3    90.0  Kumasi  100.0

Example 2. Rewrite one named feature with a thread-level transform.

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"id", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({1, 2, 3}))},
    {"sales", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({100.0, 120.0, 90.0}))},
    {"city", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_note({"Accra", "Tema", "Kumasi"}))},
});

auto out = df.transform("sales", [](const pluss::table::Thread& thread) { return thread.clip(0.0, 110.0); });
Expected output¶
id  sales  city
1   100.0  Accra
2   110.0  Tema
3    90.0  Kumasi

Example 3. Rewrite every feature with the same thread-level transform.

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"id", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({1, 2, 3}))},
    {"sales", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({100.0, 120.0, 90.0}))},
    {"city", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_note({"Accra", "Tema", "Kumasi"}))},
});

auto out = df.transform([](const pluss::table::Thread& thread) { return thread.kind() == pluss::table::ThreadKind::Series ? thread.clip(0.0, 110.0) : thread; });
Expected output¶
id  sales  city
1   100.0  Accra
2   110.0  Tema
3    90.0  Kumasi

Example 4. Rewrite one or more selected features with structured transform specs.

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"id", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({1, 2, 3}))},
    {"sales", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({100.0, 120.0, 90.0}))},
    {"city", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_note({"Accra", "Tema", "Kumasi"}))},
});

auto out = df.transform({{.feature = "sales", .expr = [](const pluss::table::Thread& thread) { return thread.clip(0.0, 110.0); }}});
Expected output¶
id  sales  city
1   100.0  Accra
2   110.0  Tema
3    90.0  Kumasi

Practical Behavior¶

  • transform(fn) rewrites every feature with the same thread-level function.

  • transform(feature, thread_fn) rewrites one existing feature in place within the returned frame.

  • transform(feature, frame_fn) is the derive-style overload: it can create a new feature from the whole frame, as long as the returned thread matches the frame case count.

truediv¶

API Signatures¶

DataFrame::truediv(other: const DataFrame&) -> DataFrame

DataFrame::truediv(other: double) -> DataFrame

Notes¶

Applies elementwise true division to compatible numeric features.

Inputs¶

other : const DataFrame& Scalar divisor or right-hand frame used for elementwise true division.

Output¶

DataFrame Value produced by this call.

Options¶

Option and enum values, when present, are listed with their effects under Inputs.

Examples¶

Example 1. Divide each compatible numeric cell against another aligned frame.

auto left = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"id", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({1, 2, 3}))},
    {"sales", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({100.0, 120.0, 90.0}))},
});
auto right = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"id", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({2, 2, 4}))},
    {"sales", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({110.0, 110.0, 100.0}))},
});

auto out = left.truediv(right);
Expected output¶
id    sales
0.5   0.909091
1.0   1.090909
0.75  0.9

Example 2. Divide each compatible numeric cell against one broadcast scalar value.

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"id", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({1, 2, 3}))},
    {"sales", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({100.0, 120.0, 90.0}))},
    {"city", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_note({"Accra", "Tema", "Kumasi"}))},
});

auto out = df.truediv(10);
Expected output¶
id  sales  city
0.1  10.0  Accra
0.2  12.0  Tema
0.3   9.0  Kumasi

Practical Behavior¶

  • Scalar truediv(...) divides every compatible numeric cell by the supplied scalar.

  • Frame-vs-frame truediv(...) divides aligned numeric features row by row.

  • Non-numeric features pass through unchanged in the scalar form and are excluded from numeric combination work.

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({
